The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of Standard normal and normal laws has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and let $\#$ be counting measure on
$(\mathbb N,\mathcal P(\mathbb N))$ ([[def-counting-measure]],
[[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]]). For every measurable
$f:\mathbb N\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb N} f\,d\#=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f(n),$$
where the right side is the nonnegative extended series of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, let $\Pi$ be a
sigma-finite measure on it, and fix a data value $y$. Let
$L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable function. Define its
**evidence normalizer** by
$$Z_\Pi(y):=\int_\Theta L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Only when $0<Z_\Pi(y)<+\infty$ define the **fiberwise posterior update** by
$$\Pi_y(A):=\frac{\int_A L_y(\theta)\,\Pi(d\theta)}{Z_\Pi(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The definition makes no quotient at zero or infinite evidence. A prior is
**proper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=1$, as in
[[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. We call a sigma-finite
prior **improper** when $\Pi(\Theta)=+\infty$; the formula also applies to
other sigma-finite measures. For an improper prior, $Z_\Pi(y)$ is a fiberwise
normalizer only; it does not by itself define a prior-predictive probability or
a conditional law.

When the data are described by a dominated experiment, the dominating measure
and its sigma-finiteness are as in
[[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]. A family of pointwise likelihood
sections is not assumed to be jointly measurable in parameter and data; that
additional condition must be supplied separately whenever Tonelli is used.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T,\Pi)$ be a measure space, let $L_y:\Theta\to[0,+\infty]$
be measurable for a fixed datum $y$, and put
$Z:=\int_\Theta L_y\,d\Pi$. For a finite positive constant $c$, the set
function
$$A\longmapsto c\int_A L_y\,d\Pi$$
is a probability measure if and only if $0<Z<+\infty$ and $c=Z^{-1}$. In
particular, if $Z=0$ or $Z=+\infty$, no finite positive scaling makes the
fiberwise update a probability measure.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

Let $X$ be a separable real Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|_X$, let $D\subseteq X$ be Borel, and let $\mu_0$ be a Borel probability on $X$ with $\mu_0(D)=1$. Here $\mathcal B(X)$ is generated by the norm-open sets. Give $D$ the relative topology and Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(D)=\{D\cap B:B\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and let $\mu_{0,D}$ be the restriction of $\mu_0$ to $D$, so $\mu_{0,D}(A)=\mu_0(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal B(D)$. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be a measurable data space. Assume $\Phi:D\times\mathsf Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is measurable from $\bigl(D\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal B(D)\otimes\mathcal Y\bigr)$ to $\bigl((-\infty,+\infty],\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])\bigr)$, where $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ is generated by the order topology on the extended real line and $\mathcal B((-\infty,+\infty])$ is its trace on $(-\infty,+\infty]$; thus $+\infty$ is allowed and $-\infty$ is excluded. Let $\mathsf Y_0\subseteq\mathsf Y$. Suppose that for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the section $u\mapsto\Phi(u;y)$ is finite and continuous as a real-valued function on $D$ with its relative topology inherited from the norm topology. Suppose there is one Borel function $M_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, independent of $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, such that
$$\Phi(u;y)\ge -M_1(\|u\|_X)\quad(u\in D,\ y\in\mathsf Y_0),\qquad \int_D e^{M_1(\|u\|_X)}\,\mu_{0,D}(du)<\infty.$$
Define $\operatorname{supp}\mu_0:=\{x\in X:\mu_0(U)>0\text{ for every open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$. Then for every $y\in\mathsf Y_0$, the evidence $Z_\Phi(y)$ is finite and strictly positive, and the normalized fiberwise update $\Pi^y$ is a probability measure on $D$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, called the **parameter space** and the **data space**. Let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty set of **admissible truths**, and let $F:U\to Y$ be a **forward map**. For $x\in U$, the datum $F(x)$ is its exact observation. For $y\in Y$, define the exact solution set

$$S_F(y):=\{x\in U:F(x)=y\}.$$

The datum $y$ is exactly solvable on $U$ when $S_F(y)\ne\varnothing$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $U$, meaning it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; truths equivalent under $\sim$ represent the same recovery target. A **metric solution-class space** for $(U,\sim)$ consists of a metric space $(Q,d_Q)$ and a function $q:U\to Q$ whose image is all of $Q$ and such that $q(x)=q(x')$ if and only if $x\sim x'$. The loss between two target classes is their metric distance $d_Q$. Exact recovery of the truth itself is the special case $Q=U$, $q(x)=x$, and $d_Q=d_X$ restricted to $U$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
Order on the natural numbers, which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$, proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $\mathbb{N}$ be the von Neumann naturals, with $0 = \varnothing$ and
$\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and let $<$ be the order of
[[def-nat-order]], so that $m < n \iff m \in n$ and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]).
Write $\approx$ for equinumerosity ([[def-equinumerous]]). Then:

1. for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there is **no injection** $\sigma(n) \to n$;
2. if $m < n$ then there is no injection $n \to m$;
3. if $n \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n = m$;
4. $\mathbb{N} \not\approx n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$;
5. no natural number is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself: if
   $A \subseteq n$ and $n \approx A$, then $A = n$.

Claim 1 is the pigeonhole principle in its sharpest form, that $n + 1$ pigeons do
not fit injectively into $n$ holes; the other four are the consequences the
library actually quotes. Claim 3 says a finite set is equinumerous with exactly
one natural number, so "the number of elements" is well defined. Claim 4 says
$\mathbb{N}$ is infinite. Claim 5 says no natural number is Dedekind-infinite.

**Why this is proved here.** The next item on this page defines finiteness as
equinumerosity with a natural number, and the three size classes it introduces
are exhaustive by construction but mutually exclusive only because of claim 4.
Several later items also need claim 3 or claim 5. The principle is elementary and
belongs with the naturals, but it is about counting rather than about order, so
it is proved here, immediately before finiteness is defined, from induction and
the identification of the order with membership alone. Nothing below uses
ordinals, cardinals, or any later material.

derivations.claim: For each $m\in\mathbb N$, the initial set $E_m=\{0,1,\ldots,m\}$ has counting measure $m+1<\infty$ by [F1] and [F2], and $\bigcup_mE_m=\mathbb N$. Thus $\mu$ is sigma-finite by [F3]. By [F16], $\mathbb N$ is infinite, so [F1] gives $\mu(\mathbb N)=+\infty$.

The counting-integral formula [F6] gives $Z(0)=\int_{\mathbb N}\frac{e^{-n^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\mu(dn)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-n^2/2}$. Its $n=0$ term is $1/\sqrt{2\pi}>0$ by [F8].

AC implies countable choice by [F5], so the normal-density interface [F4] applies: for each $n$, $N(n,1)$ is a probability law with the displayed Gaussian density. Since the parameter sigma-algebra is $\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$, every evaluation $n\mapsto N(n,1)(B)$ is measurable, and the likelihood section $n\mapsto L_y(n)$ is measurable by [F15]; thus the sampling family satisfies [F13]. The map $F(n)=n$ on the nonempty admissible set $U=\mathbb N$ satisfies the forward-map interface [F14]. By [F11] this is not a proper Bayesian model with prior $\mu$, because [step 1.1] shows the prior mass is infinite.

For every $n\ge1$, $n^2\ge n$, so monotonicity of the exponential [F8] gives $e^{-n^2/2}\le e^{-n/2}$. Let $r=e^{-1/2}$. By [F8], $0<r<1$, and [F7] makes $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r^n$ finite. Comparison of nonnegative partial sums now bounds the evidence series in step 1.2 by $1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r^n<\infty$. Hence $0<Z(0)<\infty$.

Applying [F10] to $L_0$ and the sigma-finite measure $\mu$ gives the probability with singleton masses $L_0(n)/Z(0)=e^{-n^2/2}/\sum_je^{-j^2/2}$, as stated. Its fixed-data meaning and lack of a prior-predictive probability follow from [F9]; [F11] confirms that no proper Bayesian model is supplied by this prior. The function-space propriety theorem [F12] does not apply because its prior is a probability, whereas [step 1.1] gives $\mu(\mathbb N)=+\infty$.
